content: Vaginal rings, also referred to as intravaginal rings or V-rings, are polymeric drug delivery devices with a doughnut-shaped design. These devices are engineered to provide a controlled release of medications directly to the vaginal area over an extended period of time. Currently, several vaginal ring products are available on the market: Estring: This is a low-dose estradiol-releasing ring made from silicone elastomer. It is specifically designed for the treatment of vaginal atrophy. Femring: This is another low-dose estradiol-acetate-releasing ring, also manufactured from silicone elastomer. It is used to alleviate symptoms such as hot flashes and vaginal atrophy associated with menopause. NuvaRing: This is a low-dose contraceptive vaginal ring made from poly(ethylene-co-vinyl acetate). It releases etonogestrel (a progestin) and ethinyl estradiol (an estrogen) to provide effective birth control. In addition to these existing products, several other vaginal ring formulations are currently under development. Methods of Use Vaginal rings are designed to be easily inserted and removed by the user. Once inserted, the vaginal walls hold the ring securely in place. The precise location of the ring within the vagina is not critical for its clinical effectiveness, although it is commonly positioned near the cervix. These rings are typically left in place during sexual intercourse, and most couples report no interference or discomfort. In many cases, neither partner is aware of the ring's presence. However, the ring can be removed prior to intercourse if desired. For contraceptive rings like NuvaRing, removal should not exceed one to three hours to maintain the efficacy of birth control. Femring: This ring is inserted into the vagina and left in place for three months. After this period, it is removed and replaced with a new ring. NuvaRing: This ring is inserted into the vagina and left in place for three weeks. After three weeks, it is removed for a ring-free week to allow for menstruation. Vaginal Ring Updates Advancements in vaginal ring technology are currently being explored for the controlled release of microbicides and vaccines aimed at preventing HIV infection. However, concerns have been raised regarding the biodegradability of these products, particularly in light of growing environmental concerns about pollution and the use of plastics. This issue is especially relevant for rings made from poly(ethylene-co-vinyl acetate) and similar materials.
